question: Tell me about TeachSpark.
answer: TeachSpark is a WhatsApp bot Tushar built solo in August 2026 for time-poor Indian K–12 teachers. It started with one real teacher, his mother, who teaches Sanskrit. Instead of doing the task for teachers, it teaches the reusable AI skill: a teacher makes a differentiated worksheet herself in about two minutes, sees the time she saved, and comes back for the next skill. The idea is “capability, not dependency.” The first-week pilot (snapshot 24 Aug 2026, test handsets excluded) brought 17 teachers on, activated 8, and saved a median 37.5 self-reported minutes each. It runs as a live pilot on a Twilio sandbox; uptime after 9 Sep 2026 is unverified.

question: Tell me about RailCite.
answer: RailCite is a trust-first assistant Tushar built solo in Aug–Sep 2026. It helps a Chief Commercial Inspector cite the right Indian Railways rule or circular, without ever inventing a citation. It answers with correctly numbered, dated citations and supersession lineage, or refuses when no passage governs the case, because refusal is designed as a success state. A validator drops any answer whose citations don't resolve, so the live corpus (5,760 documents as of 15 Sep 2026) can grow nightly without the model making one up. His father, a serving Chief Commercial Inspector, and his colleagues were its first users.

question: Tell me about Slag City.
aliases: What is the Slag City game?
Tell me about the beat-'em-up game
answer: Slag City is an original arcade beat-'em-up that runs in the browser, built the way a coin-op cabinet behaves: attract mode, insert coin, fight, a 10-second continue countdown, and initials on the hi-score table. It is one complete stage — a three-boss gauntlet, with a story told in an eight-slide intro and the boss dialogue — playable on a desktop in a simulated cabinet or on a phone with on-screen controls; coins are free. It started where Dino Arcade stops: that emulator is fine for private play but cannot be published, so the goal was a publishable brawler with wholly original IP. Tushar built it in September 2026 with Phaser 3, TypeScript and Vite, deployed on Vercel; the game logic is a pure TypeScript core with a seeded RNG, so recorded input replays are hashed in tests and a behaviour change fails a golden. It is live.

question: Tell me about Campfire Board.
aliases: Tell me about the Campfire board
answer: Campfire Board is Tushar's personal fork of Backlog.md, reshaped into a local-first, multi-project command centre for his AI build workflow: every project stays a self-contained folder of Markdown files, and one dashboard, launched locally in Chrome, renders them all. It adds a multi-project switcher, a Kanban board with an Execution / Workflow toggle, an hours-axis Execution Gantt with dependency arrows, a statistics view and an in-app artifacts viewer, all served from a single Bun-compiled local binary with the web UI embedded — nothing to deploy. A hosted live demo runs a sample project. Backlog.md is by Alex Gavrilescu and contributors (MIT licence); Campfire inherits its Markdown-native, agent-first philosophy. Built in September 2026; its status is built, with a live demo.

question: Tell me about Urja.
aliases: Tell me about the AI munshi
answer: Urja is an AI munshi for Indian small-fleet owners. An owner asks why a finished trip made almost nothing; Urja reconciles each trip's diesel, tolls and kilometres against the vehicle data and tells the owner each morning, in Hindi or English, which rupees don't add up and how sure it is. It is a solo concept by Tushar (September–October 2026) on a simulated 24-truck fleet: five deterministic rules raise every flag with a confidence level, the morning brief is templated so it never invents a figure, and one Gemini-backed Ask box answers questions with a labelled fallback. Next.js on Vercel, with a three.js reconstruction of the flagged night. It is live on the simulated fleet.
